If you're looking for ways to promote smaller subs, cross-posting content is probably the most direct and unobtrusive way to do that. Pick out some interesting content from your niche subverse and cross-post it to a relevant large sub with "(x-post /v/NicheSubverse)" in the title. You can even link to your sub in the comments if you like. That way you're providing content for the large sub, promoting small subs in an unobtrusive way, and everyone benefits.

Taking this a step farther, I try to cross-post the other way as well. Say I find a story that I'm going to post to /v/gaming, but is relevant to /v/Nintendo also. I'll post it to /v/Nintendo first and then post in /v/gaming with "(x-post /v/Nintendo)" as well. That way, the smaller sub gets content, exposure, and it didn't cost me a lot of extra effort to do. It has the additional benefit of promoting a number of smaller subs that I myself don't subscribe to, but others might be interested in.

If everyone posted to small subs and then cross-posted to the large sub they intended to post to, imagine all the niche subverses people would be exposed to on a regular basis.

No food is inherently "healthy" or "unhealthy". It's all about context, moderation, and portion size.

Ice cream in moderation is healthy because its good taste provides mental release and promotes satiety (lessening the chance to binge if you can include ice cream in your diet commonly). In excess, ice cream can also be unhealthy since it's very calorically-dense and thus easy to overeat and gain weight.

On the other hand broccoli (yes, the "king" of healthy vegetables) can be unhealthy. For example: if over-consumed, its high fiber content could cause digestive issues if you already have adequate fiber intake. Also, restricting yourself to only eating foods deemed "healthy" by the media like broccoli can promote an unhealthy relationship with food and lead to binges which are ultimately counterproductive. That being said, broccoli in quantities 99% would find palatable is probably a healthy choice.

So whole grains can be either healthy or unhealthy depending on the context. Is it the most satiating calorie-for-calorie? Probably not, but it has its place in any diet. I'm pretty much of the opinion that there's almost no food in existence that doesn't have a place in a good diet in the right context.
